		<title>A Network-on-Chip (NoC) For Multi-Die Devices</title>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Transporting the native packetized traffic of the NoC directly across die boundaries using a stable, invariant interface.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/a-network-on-chip-noc-for-multi-die-devices/">A Network-on-Chip (NoC) For Multi-Die Devices</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The semiconductor industry is rapidly transitioning from monolithic SoCs to chiplet-based architectures. At the same time, AI workloads are evolving beyond cloud inference into physical AI: systems that perceive, reason, and act in the real world. Autonomous vehicles, industrial robots, humanoid robots, drones, and intelligent manufacturing systems all require continuous, high-volume data flow between heterogeneous compute engines.</p>
<p>However, these two trends expose a weakness in today’s die-to-die communication architectures. While coherent interconnect protocols have been highly successful for processor-centric systems, they are fundamentally mismatched to the traffic patterns generated by modern AI accelerators.</p>
<p>As a result, a new approach is needed that involves transporting the native packetized traffic of the NoC directly across die boundaries using a stable, invariant interface.</p>
<h2>Physical AI changes the nature of on-chip communication</h2>
<p>Traditional processors are dominated by memory accesses, synchronization, and cache coherence. Physical AI systems are different. A modern automotive compute platform may simultaneously execute:</p>
<ul>
<li>Multiple camera processing pipelines</li>
<li>Radar and lidar signal processing</li>
<li>Sensor fusion</li>
<li>AI perception networks</li>
<li>Localization and mapping</li>
<li>Path planning</li>
<li>Functional safety monitoring</li>
<li>Vehicle actuator control</li>
</ul>
<p>Rather than exchanging individual cache lines, these engines often exchange continuous streams of feature maps, tensors, point clouds, video frames, and intermediate inference results. These data streams often consist of hundreds of kilobytes, or even megabytes, moving between specialized accelerators at deterministic rates. The communication pattern resembles a high-performance dataflow network more than a coherent symmetric multi-processor system. As physical AI systems become more capable, the amount of accelerator-to-accelerator traffic continues to grow faster than CPU-to-memory traffic.</p>
<h2>Where coherent protocols excel</h2>
<p>Coherent die-to-die protocols remain the right solution for many applications and perform exceptionally well for:</p>
<ul>
<li>Coherent communication between processor dies in large SMP systems</li>
<li>CPU memory accesses</li>
<li>Synchronization</li>
<li>Control-plane communication from CPUs to I/O management processors or accelerators</li>
</ul>
<p>These protocols were designed to maintain memory consistency while moving relatively small cache-line-sized transactions. For processor-centric workloads sharing memory, they are extremely effective.</p>
<h2>Why are they inefficient for AI data movement?</h2>
<p>Accelerator traffic follows very different patterns. Most coherent protocols divide communication into cache-line-sized transactions, typically 64 bytes each. Every cache line carries protocol overhead, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>Addresses</li>
<li>Transaction identifiers</li>
<li>Ordering information</li>
<li>Response tracking</li>
<li>Coherence metadata</li>
</ul>
<p>When transferring large tensors or feature maps, this overhead must be repeated thousands of times. For AI workloads, the actual payload accounts for only a portion of the transmitted bandwidth, with protocol overhead consuming an increasingly significant fraction of the available die-to-die bandwidth.</p>
<p>Some coherent protocols have added optimizations to help improve the efficiency of non-coherent, bursty traffic. While useful, these mechanisms are limited in scope. For example, they span only a small number of beats and cannot fully ameliorate the overhead associated with very long streaming transfers of arbitrary data. As accelerator bandwidth increases into the terabytes-per-second range inside future automotive AI systems, repeatedly transmitting cache-line metadata becomes increasingly difficult to justify.</p>
<h2>Existing approaches</h2>
<p>Many non-coherent die-to-die approaches have been proposed, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>AMD/Xilinx AXI Chip2Chip, which is deployed in FPGA implementations.</li>
<li>Open Chiplet Atlas (OCA) AXI over UCIe (AoU), a proposal from Tenstorrent/OCA.</li>
<li>Various proprietary approaches that serialize AXI over high-speed serial interfaces.</li>
</ul>
<p>These approaches extend AXI interfaces across die boundaries and work well for connecting peripherals and control-oriented IP. However, they still operate at the transaction layer. Each NoC packet of each virtual channel must be converted into AXI transactions before crossing the die boundary, then reconstructed as NoC packets on the receiving side. As systems scale to dozens of AI engines across multiple chiplets, this repeated conversion adds unnecessary latency, buffering, and implementation complexity.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281897" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arteris_NoC-for-Multi-Die-Devices-fig1-scaled.webp?resize=2560%2C1273&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="2560" height="1273" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arteris_NoC-for-Multi-Die-Devices-fig1-scaled.webp?w=2560&amp;ssl=1 2560w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arteris_NoC-for-Multi-Die-Devices-fig1-scaled.webp?resize=300%2C149&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arteris_NoC-for-Multi-Die-Devices-fig1-scaled.webp?resize=1024%2C509&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arteris_NoC-for-Multi-Die-Devices-fig1-scaled.webp?resize=768%2C382&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arteris_NoC-for-Multi-Die-Devices-fig1-scaled.webp?resize=1536%2C764&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arteris_NoC-for-Multi-Die-Devices-fig1-scaled.webp?resize=2048%2C1019&amp;ssl=1 2048w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arteris_NoC-for-Multi-Die-Devices-fig1-scaled.webp?resize=600%2C298&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Multi-die interconnect in physical AI applications. Source: </strong><a href="https://bit.ly/3KcLBOH"><strong>Arteris, Inc</strong></a><strong>.</strong></p>
<h2>Direct NoC-to-NoC communication</h2>
<p>A more natural architecture is to allow the NoC itself to span multiple dies. Instead of terminating the NoC at each chiplet boundary, native NoC packets are transported directly across the die-to-die interface. The remote die simply becomes another portion of the same logical network. This provides several important advantages:</p>
<ul>
<li>Streaming transfers remain packetized from producer to consumer without being repeatedly converted into cache-line transactions and AXI interfaces. Protocol overhead is amortized across long data streams rather than repeated for every cache line.</li>
<li>Virtual channels enable multiple traffic classes, including control traffic, real-time sensor data, AI inference traffic, and bulk DMA transfers, to share the same physical die-to-die connection while maintaining quality of service (QoS).</li>
<li>Existing NoC routing, arbitration, congestion management, and QoS mechanisms naturally extend across multiple dies.</li>
<li>Multiple protocols can be transported over the same die-to-die interface: for example, AXI, APB, AHB or OCP.</li>
<li>Most importantly, the die boundary ceases to be a protocol translation point. It simply becomes an additional hop in a single, multi-die network-on-chip.</li>
</ul>
<h2>Why does this matter for automotive physical AI?</h2>
<p>Automotive AI places unique demands on interconnects. Unlike cloud AI systems, automotive platforms must satisfy strict latency, determinism, power, and functional safety requirements while operating within tight thermal limits. Centralized vehicle compute platforms will integrate multiple AI chiplets connected through advanced packaging technologies. Individual chiplets may specialize in:</p>
<ul>
<li>Vision processing</li>
<li>Neural network inference</li>
<li>Radar processing</li>
<li>Lidar processing</li>
<li>CPU clusters</li>
<li>Safety and security islands</li>
<li>Memory expansion</li>
<li>Networking</li>
</ul>
<p>The largest traffic flows are often not between CPUs and memory but between accelerators themselves. For example:</p>
<ul>
<li>Camera processing → AI perception → Sensor fusion → Planning → Vehicle control</li>
<li>Shared tensor movement between multiple neural-network accelerators</li>
</ul>
<p>These are fundamentally streaming dataflow applications. Transporting these streams using a native packetized NoC enables far more efficient bandwidth utilization, while reducing latency and buffering throughout the system. The result is higher sustained throughput, lower energy consumption per transferred bit, and greater scalability as additional accelerator chiplets are added.</p>
<h2>The challenge of exposing internal NoC protocols</h2>
<p>Despite these advantages, directly exposing an implementation’s internal NoC protocol is problematic. Internal packet formats frequently evolve as NoC implementations gain new capabilities, such as:</p>
<ul>
<li>Improved routing algorithms</li>
<li>New arbitration policies</li>
<li>Additional virtual channels</li>
<li>Enhanced QoS mechanisms</li>
<li>Updated packet formats</li>
</ul>
<p>Even relatively small NoC changes can significantly alter the internal protocol, making long-term die-to-die compatibility challenging. Routing introduces another challenge. Packet routing information may depend on the topology of the destination NoC. If the topology changes, routing vectors or addressing schemes may need to be updated. Without architectural stability, every NoC revision risks requiring die-to-die interface updates. While this may be manageable when a single team designs all dies, it becomes impractical when teams work independently.</p>
<h2>An invariant NoC interface</h2>
<p>The solution is to define an invariant architectural interface, rather than exposing the evolving internal NoC implementation. An invariant, die-to-die NoC interface provides a stable packet protocol specifically designed for die-to-die transport while allowing each chiplet’s internal NoC implementation to continue evolving independently.</p>
<p>Such an interface can:</p>
<ul>
<li>Support multiple non-coherent protocols over a single NoC transport layer.</li>
<li>Define a stable packet format.</li>
<li>Support configurable interface widths to scale bandwidth.</li>
<li>Support virtual channels for multiple traffic classes.</li>
<li>Preserve NoC routing semantics while abstracting implementation details.</li>
<li>Isolate future NoC enhancements from the die-to-die interface.</li>
<li>Facilitate a choice of physical layer implementation: for example, UCIe, BoW, PCIe or a vendor-specific PHY.</li>
</ul>
<p>This enables chiplets from different product generations to communicate through a stable architectural interface, while allowing incremental change on either side of the die-to-die boundary.</p>
<h2>Efficiency and scalability for future AI systems</h2>
<p>We propose a multi-die NoC packet transport interface based on an invariant die-to-die NoC interface. Instead of transporting cache-line transactions or extending AXI buses, the interface carries native, protocol-independent NoC packets directly between chiplets using a stable, implementation-independent packet format. The interface can be sized to match the bandwidth requirements of future AI systems, supports virtual channels for efficient sharing among diverse traffic types, and extends NoC routing seamlessly across die boundaries.</p>
<p>For physical AI, particularly in next-generation automotive computing platforms, this approach aligns the communication architecture with the system&#8217;s dominant traffic pattern: high-bandwidth, low-latency accelerator-to-accelerator data movement. By eliminating unnecessary protocol translation and minimizing transaction overhead, it creates a scalable, multi-protocol, multi-die interconnect capable of supporting increasingly complex AI pipelines, while maintaining the determinism, efficiency, and long-term architectural stability required for safety-critical deployments.</p>
<p>Learn more about <a href="https://hubs.ly/Q03sxzTc0">Arteris’ multi-die solution</a>.</p>

		<title>Managing 3D-IC Design And IP</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/managing-3d-ic-design-and-ip/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/managing-3d-ic-design-and-ip/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Keith Felton]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 24 Sep 2026 07:05:05 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[A System Perspective]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Design data management, traceability, and revision control are critical for multi-chiplet heterogeneous integration.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/managing-3d-ic-design-and-ip/">Managing 3D-IC Design And IP</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>By Keith Felton and Todd Burkholder</strong></p>
<p>The trend towards multi-chiplet heterogeneous integration is here to stay. It promises faster innovation, more powerful and specialized devices, and greater design flexibility. However, realizing its potential hinges on our ability to manage the complexity that comes with it.</p>
<p>However, with this newfound modularity comes a significant challenge: managing the vast and intricate web of data that defines these systems. This is where robust data management and meticulous data traceability become not just beneficial, but essential. Without data management, even the most brilliant multi-chiplet design can quickly become a tangled mess, leading to costly errors, delays, and a loss of confidence in the final product.</p>
<p>In the first three articles of this series (published in the <a href="https://semiengineering.com/realizing-the-future-of-3d-ic-design/">June</a>, <a href="https://semiengineering.com/realizing-the-future-of-3d-ic-final-scenario-and-sign-off/">July</a> and <a href="https://semiengineering.com/streamlining-3d-ic-design-substrate-finalization-and-tapeout/">August</a> editions of Semiconductor Engineering), we covered the first seven steps toward streamlining your 3D-IC design process. This article focuses on design data and design IP management, traceability, and revision control. This is a critical step for multi-chiplet heterogeneous integration, as there is so much design data and IP involved that using an incorrect version or missing an ECO can mean product failure.</p>
<p>Data management can be broken down to four components that will help you streamline your 3D-IC design flow:</p>
<ul>
<li>Management of the many sources of design IP</li>
<li>Design hierarchy with revision control and history tracking</li>
<li>A centralized data and information hub</li>
<li>Instant status tracking and analysis</li>
</ul>
<h2>A plethora of IP</h2>
<p>In the world of multi-chiplet design, we often bring together various pieces of IP from different sources—from internal teams, external vendors, or even open-source initiatives. Each piece of design IP comes with its own set of design files, specifications, and usage guidelines.</p>
<p>When you have multiple chiplets from different sources, potentially designed with different tools and at different times, the sheer volume and diversity of this data can be overwhelming. Without a well-defined data management strategy to manage these diverse sources, the risk of introducing defects is significantly higher.</p>
<p>Innovator3D IC Data Management software supports robust data and design IP management to provide single moment-of-truth management of design IP data. It treats the design itself as a work-in-progress, applying a revision-controlled and access-rights managed process at every stage of design, all the way to tape out.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281892" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Siemens_Managing-3D-IC-Design-and-IP-fig1.webp?resize=1919%2C1082&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1919" height="1082" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Siemens_Managing-3D-IC-Design-and-IP-fig1.webp?w=1919&amp;ssl=1 1919w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Siemens_Managing-3D-IC-Design-and-IP-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C169&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Siemens_Managing-3D-IC-Design-and-IP-fig1.webp?resize=1024%2C577&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Siemens_Managing-3D-IC-Design-and-IP-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C433&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Siemens_Managing-3D-IC-Design-and-IP-fig1.webp?resize=1536%2C866&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Siemens_Managing-3D-IC-Design-and-IP-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C338&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Innovator3D IC Data Management’s centralized cockpit.</strong></p>
<h2>Managing design hierarchy</h2>
<p>Multi-chiplet designs inherently involve a complex hierarchy. Chiplets are integrated into a larger multi-chiplet heterogeneous assembly using interposers and substrates. Managing this hierarchy effectively, especially with the inevitable design iterations, requires a powerful revision control system. When you manage your design hierarchy with revision control and history tracking, you avoid errors. Revision control is like a time machine for your designs. It allows you to track every change, revert to previous versions, and allow different teams to work on separate features or bug fixes concurrently without interfering with each other. Once a team’s work is complete and verified, their changes can be merged back into the main design.</p>
<p>Without this meticulous historical tracking, understanding how a design evolved, diagnosing issues, or even just knowing which version is currently &#8220;in play&#8221; becomes a monumental task. Errors can appear through miscommunication or accidental overwriting, leading to significant delays and increased costs. A well-managed design hierarchy with robust revision control is fundamental to preventing these types of errors.</p>
<h2>Centralized data and information hub</h2>
<p>In a distributed design environment, where different teams might be working on different chiplets across various locations, having a single, centralized hub for all design data is invaluable. This hub acts as the single source of truth, providing direct access to all relevant information for authorized personnel.</p>
<p>When engineers can quickly access information they need, cycle times are dramatically reduced. This direct access speeds up design, verification, and debugging processes, leading to faster time-to-market.</p>
<h2>Instant status tracking and analysis</h2>
<p>Beyond just storing data, an effective data management system provides real-time visibility into a project&#8217;s status. This capability is crucial for efficient project management, especially in the complex landscape of multi-chiplet integration.</p>
<p>Instant access to status tracking and analytical data empowers project managers and engineering leads to make informed decisions, proactively address issues, and ensure that the project stays on track. It transforms data from a passive record into an active tool for driving project success.</p>
<p>By embracing robust data management practices, including diligent management of the design and its IP sources, meticulous revision control, centralized information hubs, and comprehensive status tracking for traceability, you establish a solid foundation for success. These “unseen architects” ensure that your multi-chiplet designs are not only functional and perform well, but also are reliable, maintainable, and auditable — allowing you to build the complex, interconnected systems of tomorrow with confidence and clarity.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Specialization and orchestration are becoming more important as the role of AI agents in chip design widens, but coordination, control, and trust remain challenging.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/when-ai-agents-cross-chip-design-silos/">When AI Agents Cross Chip Design Silos</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Chip design is moving toward specialized AI agents working together.</li>
<li>Orchestration, integration, and guardrails are becoming critical.</li>
<li>Human engineers still play a central role in guiding and validating designs and processes.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>AI agents are becoming smarter, more capable, and increasingly optimized for specific tasks, creating new opportunities to use smaller language models instead of relying on large language models for every task.</p>
<p>This shift has broad implications for the semiconductor industry, from the actual design and manufacturing of chips to how those chips function under different workloads. While LLMs can deploy swarms of agents for continuous reasoning and independent action, that&#8217;s overkill for most applications.</p>
<p>But reducing the size of the model, and potentially the number or capability of the agents, adds its own challenges. One approach is to divide complex workflows among smaller language models and agents, while still retaining the compute capability needed to design, optimize, floor-plan, verify, and debug chips, and to identify anomalies and variations in manufacturing processes that might limit yield. This approach combines both human expertise with AI&#8217;s ability to crunch massive amounts of data.</p>
<p>&#8220;In our early work on agents, which we created for each of our tools, we have questions and answers,&#8221; said Prith Banerjee, senior vice president of innovation at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>. &#8220;We had an agent for this, and an agent for that. But in this world of multi-agent workflows, our customers are trying to design a chip. Maybe they&#8217;re having a problem with the PPA, and some engineers say they know exactly what changes are needed to lower the power. So they&#8217;ll do clock gating, but when you do clock gating, it increases the area. Then, someone who is the area expert will come in. This is exactly what happens in the real world, where multiple people come together and design a system with coordination. The human manager is coordinating the activities of the human agents in a multi-agent framework.&#8221;</p>
<p>The next step is how to automate and combine more of those processes, and that requires more guardrails to limit what AI can do.</p>
<p>&#8220;The model is drawing a boundary,&#8221; said Mo Faisal, CEO of <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/movellus/">Movellus</a>. &#8220;It&#8217;s like, &#8216;Hey, you&#8217;re getting in the domain that I work in. Stay in your lane.&#8217; We will specialize. A couple of [huge] companies will take the LLMs, but everybody else has to specialize. And AI, by the way, is not just LLMs. That&#8217;s the biggest use, but it&#8217;s not the definition of AI. AI intelligence can be used in many areas. People are building AI for chips, but there&#8217;s also AI for everything — accounting, lawyers, weather prediction, and all of those are different and unique workloads. But you don&#8217;t need to use LLMs for weather prediction. That&#8217;s inefficient.&#8221;</p>
<p>The good and bad of specialization is that agents need to be configured and integrated into existing tools and workflows. Making all of that work seamlessly is hard work. It requires orchestration by other agents, or teams of agents, that have been trained to fit together these potentially overlapping steps. And it requires a whole different way of approaching the problem, where CPU-based orchestration may be as important, if not more important, than GPU-based multiply-accumulate operations.</p>
<p>&#8220;We&#8217;ve gone to the aggregation level with &#8216;super agents,&#8217; and we think their complexity and the amount of value they can deliver is as big or bigger than EDA tools,&#8221; said Matt Graham, senior group director of verification software product management at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/cadence-design-systems/">Cadence</a>. &#8220;These are a new category of tools, and we&#8217;re starting to talk less about agents than skills that are dynamically assembled into agents. But the idea is that it&#8217;s all handled by a kind of orchestrating super-agent. And just like our customers have always arranged our tools into flows with their own custom scripting, they&#8217;re going to arrange our super agents and agentic workflows and solutions the way they need by writing their own scripts and putting them into a flow.&#8221;</p>
<p>Those super agents (or lead agents, managing agents, or just agents — this is so new that naming conventions are constantly changing), as well as sub-agents that are managed by those super-agents, and they can be used in tandem or managed separately.</p>
<p>&#8220;You can have sub-agents do different things, and then for other things we have a multi-agent solution,&#8221; said William Wang, CEO of <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/alpha-design-ai-chipagents/">ChipAgents</a>. &#8220;We released a multi-agent solution to the industry in Q4 of last year, and it&#8217;s multi-agent coordination for things like debugging. If your SoC is so big, how are you going to optimize the performance? To do that, you need multiple agents with parallel access to different contexts to do the job. Similarly, with functional/formal verification, you can have multiple agents looking at different color groups to do the debugging and be able to optimize. Those are extremely critical.&#8221;</p>
<p><strong>The integration problem</strong><br />
Chip design and manufacturing require repeatability and predictability, but many of the leading-edge chips are unique. This is particularly true for multi-die assemblies, which are often optimized for specific data types or applications, such as data centers, smartphones, and robotics. At the same time, whatever actions agents take need to be compatible with existing tools, flows, or processes, which must adapt to the rapid evolution of agentic AI.</p>
<p>&#8220;Typically, customers will work within a platform, and that could be Cadence Virtuoso, Synopsys Custom Compiler, or Keysight Advanced Design system, and within that environment we guide them through an application-specific workflow,&#8221; said Niels Faché, senior vice president at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/keysight-technologies/">Keysight EDA</a>. &#8220;We have in-product documentation to explain all the different steps, setups, and possibilities of the tools. That&#8217;s all designed for human engineers to collaborate and work on complex products. With AI, that&#8217;s becoming a very different model where human engineers work with digital engineers or agents. So now we have to redesign our products. You&#8217;ve heard about MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, where we look at a product and ask, &#8216;How can we now modularize it, provide access to different capabilities with the proper APIs?&#8217; All of that coding is typically done in Python, and that would then allow an agent to stitch together a code-based workflow. Our job is to make sure that our customers get this MCP functionality.&#8221;</p>
<p>Making that approach work requires better-defined goals for agents to work both independently and in concert with other agents, and better training of the agents to achieve those goals. &#8220;If you want an agent to perform a certain task — it could be synthesizing a filter — you would say, &#8216;I&#8217;d like to design a filter with these characteristics, a bandpass, and this frequency range,'&#8221; Faché said. &#8220;Then this agent needs to ask, &#8216;Okay, what is a filter? How do I set up a simulation?&#8217; It will need examples. But then you also need an MCP server that allows you to break down that ask into a sequence of steps and call the right functionality to execute that step. What used to be guided in a graphical user interface is now in the form of example skills that you give to an agent and say, &#8216;This is how you execute this task.'&#8221;</p>
<p>Those agents also need to be able to break through silos where necessary, but obey limitations at other times. Some of the current concerns about rogue AI agents are due to increasingly complex queries that require AI agents to look beyond silos, which, to AI, are just virtual constructs, as well as too much agent autonomy. Using small language models and agents that are incapable of deconstructing those sandboxes or scraping the entire internet will help, so barriers are only crossed when agents are allowed to do so.</p>
<p>&#8220;There are still these silos,&#8221; said Ankur Gupta, executive vice president and head of EDA IC software at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/mentor-a-siemens-business/">Siemens EDA</a>. &#8220;There&#8217;s EDA for simulation, all the way into PLM, which is real-world deployment and operation, and facilities are all kicking in. It&#8217;s not just EDA for design verification. This is where we started talking about digital twins and having some intelligence captured. Now, that&#8217;s reality, especially when you put the LLM and SLM in the picture. You&#8217;re capturing enough information for each of these silos — the chip, the system, the simulation, the PLM system — for data ontology. LLMs and SLMs will have to work off data, and we are connecting all of that as a layer. On top of that layer is each domain, and it&#8217;s interacting with the data in this layer. But it can just as easily interact across these silos.&#8221;</p>
<p>There are business cases for this kind of behavior, as well, so there is a lot riding on solving any problems. Pulling together fab data that incorporates multiple processes can save enormous amounts of money and time in chip manufacturing. &#8220;The cost of a mistake is $500 million at 3nm and 2nm,&#8221; said Gupta. &#8220;That&#8217;s where these engines have to remain high-fidelity. We use reinforcement learning, unsupervised learning — we&#8217;ve been doing that for more than a decade. But the way we measure the result of that learning capability is whether we are still delivering a trusted outcome. That doesn&#8217;t change.&#8221;</p>
<p>Small language models are well-suited for many specialized tasks. &#8220;We are seeing that happening for specific applications that are RAG-based (retrieval-augmented generation),&#8221; said Shriniwas Kulkarni, engineering leader at SiMa. &#8220;Small language models are very efficient for specific use cases, rather than using large language models and quantizing them, and they can train them with their own data to make sure they&#8217;re very accurate.</p>
<p>Others agree. &#8220;We see people aligning to ideas about agents whose context is limited in scope, and then you have an orchestrator that is looking across this, and so you want that top-down and bottom-up together as you&#8217;re building your agent architecture,&#8221; said Saurabh Gayen, chief solutions architect at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/baya-systems/">Baya Systems</a>. &#8220;What&#8217;s often missed when we&#8217;re talking about these things is a human in the loop. If you have a black-box view of the entire problem, do you build some black box that is hierarchical to get the best result, or do you want to pause as you go through this process and have a human understand so they can bake into it, &#8216;Hey, don&#8217;t think about it this way. Think about it that way.&#8217; AI isn&#8217;t so much a replacement for engineers as a way to enhance what they&#8217;re able to do and their understanding.&#8221;</p>
<p>Human engineers effectively are the glue that makes AI work. They are essential to figuring out how agents at different layers of a design, or a stack of manufacturing processes, are best optimized together. &#8220;We&#8217;re all learning this together,&#8221; Gayen said. &#8220;How you engineer those layers of agents is an art. And if somebody says they&#8217;ve found the perfect solution, that&#8217;s really just one among many.&#8221;</p>
<p>But human engineers are also in short supply. &#8220;We went through the wonderful dot-com period where nobody went into semiconductors because they all wanted to be software programmers,&#8221; said Michal Siwinski, chief product and marketing officer at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/arterisip/">Arteris</a>. &#8220;There was a lull in the talent pool, which has been recovering slowly, but there&#8217;s still a gap in terms of the number of experienced people who actually impact designs. Agentic AI helps to fill some of those voids. In this case, it&#8217;s not actually an accelerant. It&#8217;s backfilling. How many weekends can someone work on these projects?&#8221;</p>
<p><strong>The data crush</strong><br />
At the root of all these challenges and advances are changes in the way data is utilized. Concerns about sandbox break-throughs, reverse engineering, and even the performance and power draw of AI chips are all dependent on the creation, movement, storage, and security of data. Real-world data is better, but synthetic data can approximate it with better training by expert engineers.</p>
<p>&#8220;There are new classes of jobs where, if you are a top 1% expert in any area, you can get a job talking to LLMs,&#8221; noted Movellus&#8217; Faisal.</p>
<p>Models will follow, and agents will deploy them. &#8220;The fabs aren&#8217;t generating these AI models yet,&#8221; said Wally Rhines, CEO of <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/silvaco-inc/">Silvaco</a>. &#8220;Everyone wants to use Claude for everything. People are simulating all sorts of stuff. The difference here is that in physical processes, you have basic device physics that controls the effects of changing a process. We have years of SPICE modeling and BSIM models. We have TCAD engineers who talk in a language called Jump, and they are a culture unto themselves and tend to continue doing things the way they&#8217;ve done them. What you need are innovative people who can generate real models from synthetic data that can be calibrated with real data to build a virtual model.&#8221;</p>
<p>&#8220;In some cases, you&#8217;d really rather sell an agent than software,&#8221; Rhines said. &#8220;It&#8217;s not clear if anybody in EDA is actually pricing based upon tokens rather than traditional pricing models. I don&#8217;t think anyone is, but their customers are all talking about it. Selling an agent that will automate the calibration and jump back to my store of synthetic simulated data against the physical data. We don&#8217;t get to see the physical data, but we do know how many tokens our agents consume, so it&#8217;s a way that EDA can sell a product, get the benefit, and no one sees the underlying data that companies want to keep proprietary.&#8221;</p>
<p><strong>The future</strong><br />
Some of the changes underway with AI look very familiar.</p>
<p>&#8220;You can draw parallels to the early 2000s, when the gigahertz wars all of a sudden became multicore,&#8221; said Movellus&#8217; Faisal. &#8220;Everything was going to be a GPU, and then, &#8216;No, it&#8217;s going to be CPUs and GPUs.&#8217; We go through the same architectural churn every 10 or 15 years. The big difference is that back then, a chip was whatever you could do at reticle size. Now the chip is the whole data center. You may have many GPUs working together like one chip. So the bottleneck will shift to data movement, and then it will move to something else once we solve that.&#8221;</p>
<p>What&#8217;s different, though, is how the pieces are being assembled and how they will be used in the future. &#8220;We can talk about how great agentic flows are in terms of how much they improve productivity, and there&#8217;s a whole orchestration conversation,&#8221; said Arteris&#8217; Siwinski. &#8220;You have multi-agent solutions where you orchestrate across domains, which is very interesting because you&#8217;re trying to get the analog designer and the verification person and the formal person talking the same language. Hopefully, with agentic AI, that becomes easier because there&#8217;s a common understanding of something. The smart edge is coming, and you will have really good reasons to optimize and to create more unique software.&#8221;</p>
<p>The big unknown is where and how exactly engineers will fit into this AI agent-filled world. All indications are that their expertise will still be needed, but how their jobs will change isn&#8217;t clear.</p>
<p>&#8220;With multi-agent coordination, in the future we&#8217;re going to have virtual chip companies that are also going to be virtual AI engineers working together and collaborating to form this agent organization,&#8221; said ChipAgents&#8217; Wang. &#8220;Then, maybe part of the chip companies will be virtual in the future. If you look at physical AI and robotics, one of the reasons why robotics has not taken off yet is that they don&#8217;t have specialized chips. If I open the refrigerator door, it takes a second. A robot takes 20 seconds. So people gave up. But in the future, robotic companies will build their own ASICs. The chip engine, this kind of AI platform, will be very important to enable these physical AI robot companies. They can all build the chips themselves.&#8221;</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/when-ai-agents-cross-chip-design-silos/">When AI Agents Cross Chip Design Silos</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>AI may accelerate semiconductor design, but users still need formal proof, semantic continuity, and auditable workflows to trust automation. </p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/edas-future-is-evidence-driven-automation/">EDA’s Future Is Evidence-Driven Automation</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways</strong>:</p>
<ul>
<li>AI’s biggest EDA opportunity is workflow-level orchestration that coordinates tools, people, constraints, and domain knowledge across traditionally fragmented design stages, rather than merely improving individual tools.</li>
<li>Trust requires evidence and semantic continuity. AI-generated recommendations or assertions must preserve design intent and remain independently verifiable through deterministic verification, formal proof, reproducibility, and audit trails.</li>
<li>The emerging EDA model is human-guided, agentic automation. AI handles repetitive coordination, exploration, debugging, and handoffs, while engineers retain control over specifications and signoff. Established EDA engines provide the ground truth.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>AI is arriving in EDA at a time when engineers can no longer depend on brute-force scaling for performance and power improvements, and when the gaps created by disconnected point tools are becoming increasingly time-consuming to fill.</p>
<p>As designs expand to tens of billions of transistors and incorporate chiplets in multi-die assemblies, the hardest problems increasingly sit between tools — preserving intent, managing interdependencies, and identifying potential failures before they reach tapeout. At advanced nodes, where design costs can reach hundreds of millions of dollars and a single respin can threaten an entire program, AI&#8217;s real value will depend on whether it can accelerate various steps in the design flow while organizing and interpreting the data needed to trust the results.</p>
<p>The balance is between reliability and practicality. The global shortage of skilled engineers has not gone away. But it has made workflow automation more attractive, provided it can either improve the productivity of human engineers or achieve comparable results.</p>
<p>“Every customer is saying, ‘Give me the ability to shrink my time to results by at least 2×,’” said Ankur Gupta, executive vice president and head of EDA IC software at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/mentor-a-siemens-business/">Siemens EDA</a>. “Demand is pushing EDA toward a new operating model built on faster engines, smarter execution, and trusted outcomes. Acceleration may come from GPUs, machine learning, or reinforcement learning, but the larger goal is to shorten design cycles without losing confidence in the result.”</p>
<p>Efficiency also matters at the agent layer. Allowing any agent to call any tool may be flexible, but it can be expensive and inefficient if the underlying interfaces are poorly written. The goal is to do more of that integration work in advance so customers can either use a vendor&#8217;s agents or their own without paying unnecessary token and orchestration costs.</p>
<p>The economics of AI are becoming increasingly important as engineers incorporate it at various places in the design process.</p>
<p>“If I spend more money on tokens than a human would cost, then it doesn&#8217;t make sense,&#8221; said Thomas Andersen, vice president of the AI Excellence Group at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>. “Agentic AI is useful only when it reduces the cost and complexity of production workflows. An agentic loop can perform sequences of tasks that an expert would otherwise handle manually, from automating repetitive steps to coordinating work across tools. Everybody wants to automate their workflows. They want agentic automation because that&#8217;s their way to productivity, to faster tape-out cycles, cutting costs, everything.”</p>
<p>The hard part isn&#8217;t dropping a tool. It&#8217;s integrating agents into real customers&#8217; design flows.</p>
<p><b>Current challenges</b><br />
Semiconductor design is inherently a multi-tool process, spanning architecture, IP configuration, integration, verification, implementation, and sign-off. The challenge is not simply moving data from one tool to another, but preserving the design intent, assumptions, and engineering context behind that data. “At the system level, where connectivity, address maps, performance constraints, and security requirements must remain consistent across many IP blocks and, increasingly, across multiple dies, engineers often serve as the integration layer,” explained Andy Nightingale, vice president of product management and marketing at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/arterisip/">Arteris</a>.</p>
<p>That becomes increasingly difficult as systems grow in complexity. “The same architectural intent may be represented differently across integration, performance analysis, verification, and implementation environments,” Nightingale said. “If those representations diverge, the result can be additional verification cycles, manual rework, and late discovery of system-level issues. Better optimization between tools therefore needs to provide semantic continuity across the design flow, not simply file-format interoperability.”</p>
<p>Still, AI’s real impact on EDA will be less about sign-off and more about streamlining the peripheral process and data-management work around the flow. “There’s as much value there now as in the core simulators and layout tools, and that’s where AI can help you get things done much faster,” said Chris Mueth, new opportunities business manager at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/keysight-technologies/">Keysight EDA</a>.</p>
<p>Chip design is essentially a relay race involving dozens of specialized tools, including architectural exploration, RTL, lint, clock-domain crossing, formal, simulation, synthesis, place-and-route, timing and power sign-off, physical verification, equivalence checking, DFT, and post-silicon correlation.</p>
<p>“Each was written by a different vendor, against a different data model, with different assumptions about what ‘done’ means,” said Ashish Darbari, CEO of <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/axiomise/">Axiomise</a>. “The relay is where most of the pain lives. As the <a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2606.19795v1">Agentic Electronic Design Automation: A Handoff Perspective</a> survey puts it, EDA is ‘inherently multi-stage and handoff-heavy,’ and every artifact crosses tool, session, and organizational boundaries before signoff. Each transfer is a chance to lose information, silently reinterpret intent, or push a decision that was locally optimal in one tool into a globally suboptimal position downstream.”</p>
<p>Darbari groups the core workflow challenges into a few recurring failure modes:</p>
<ul>
<li><b>No shared semantic model.</b> Synthesis, P&amp;R, and signoff are still optimized for local objectives because they cannot reliably see downstream consequences. Integrated platforms help within one vendor stack, but semantic gaps remain wide across vendors and between design and verification.</li>
<li><b>Handoff loss between design and verification.</b> RTL often carries intent that never makes it into machine-checkable form, forcing engineers to re-derive testbenches, assertions, coverage models, constraints, and waivers from ambiguous English. <a href="https://semiengineering.com/first-time-silicon-success-plummets/">Silicon success data</a> underscores the cost. First-time silicon success has fallen sharply, with most respins still traced to design errors. That is a workflow and intent-transfer problem, not simply a compute problem.</li>
<li><b>Fragmented data formats and closed databases.</b> A common, vendor-neutral data model is still missing, so cross-tool AI efforts often begin by rebuilding parsers instead of applying intelligence to the design problem.</li>
<li><b>The reconciliation tax.</b> Engineers spend significant time reconciling constraints, waivers, timing exceptions, coverage exclusions, and floorplan intent between adjacent tools. Much of that work is bookkeeping to keep the flow coherent, not verification itself.</li>
<li><b>Local optima, global pain.</b> A tool can meet its local target while creating downstream closure problems, such as a congestion-hostile netlist or a hold issue that triggers another ECO loop. The opportunity is to optimize across boundaries, not just within them.</li>
<li><b>Trustworthy EDA.</b> Tools also have bugs, including signoff tools. Pardalos, Donaldson, Morini, Pozzi, and Wickerson’s <a href="https://www.doc.ic.ac.uk/~afd/papers/2024/DVCon.pdf">Who checks the checkers?</a> paper showed that Equifuzz uncovered 16 distinct bugs across three major commercial C-to-RTL equivalence checkers, including unsoundness cases where non-equivalent designs were declared equivalent. The lesson reaches beyond equivalence checking: AI can automate handoffs only if it preserves not just data, but the assumptions, limits, and evidential status of each result.</li>
</ul>
<p>That is why the next phase of AI in EDA is shifting from optimizing individual tools to coordinating the people, engines, and domain knowledge that sit between them.</p>
<p>Solaiman Rahim, chief product officer at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/alpha-design-ai-chipagents/">ChipAgents</a>, said tool-level AI has already improved individual engines, but the larger opportunity is coordinating the dependencies between tools and people. A DFT engineer, for example, may complete insertion correctly but still need timing analysis, expert interpretation, and another round of fixes before the work is usable. Each handoff can add days. “If you have a DFT agent handling DFT insertion and a timing agent that runs timing and debugs timing, these two agents can work together to speed up the process,” Rahim said. “Instead of taking weeks, it can take potentially just hours.”</p>
<p>That speedup requires more than scripts. Workflows need access to methodology, design knowledge, and context accumulated across teams. Rahim described an ontology layer that can capture why expert engineers avoid certain cells, choose particular constraints, or debug recurring failures, then make that know-how available to less experienced users and to coordinated AI workflows.</p>
<p>The same need for workflow-level coordination shows up outside the core digital flow, particularly where physical analysis depends on moving design data, assumptions, and results across multiple engineering domains. Satish Radhakrishnan, head of go-to-market for semiconductor and electronics at Vinci, said physics-based analysis faces the same workflow problem. Specialized tools may work well on their own, but model preparation, data movement, specialist handoffs, and result interpretation still slow the loop. By the time the analysis returns, the design may already have changed.</p>
<p>The problem grows as chips, packages, and systems become more tightly coupled. A chip-level change can affect package and board temperatures, mechanical stress, warpage, and reliability, none of which respects the boundary between tools or teams.</p>
<p>Radhakrishnan said much of the delay occurs before a solver starts. Engineers still clean geometry, create meshes, apply materials and boundary conditions, and hand results between design and simulation specialists. That process may support scheduled analysis, but it cannot provide reliable feedback each time a design changes. The goal, he said, is to move from isolated simulation checkpoints to continuous physics reasoning inside the design workflow.</p>
<p><b>Where EDA workflows are headed</b><br />
ChipAgent’s Rahim predicts that the next layer of AI assistance will depend on understanding design intent, not just parsing cells and wires. “In SoC debug, for example, an AI system that understands the instruction being executed, the memory operation involved, and the relevant cycles in a waveform can help narrow a failure the way an expert designer would. The value comes from pairing intent recognition with an intelligence layer that can take action across the workflow.”</p>
<p>As part of this, requirements management is essential. “Today’s AI still has room for error, so you don’t let it own specifications or sign-off,&#8221; said Keysight&#8217;s Meuth. &#8220;You use it to accelerate the workflow around those decisions, not to make the decisions themselves.”</p>
<p>These safeguards are being implemented wherever AI is used. Paul Graykowski, director of product marketing at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/cadence-design-systems/">Cadence</a>, pointed to one guardrail for AI-assisted testbench enhancement. Rather than allowing an agent to rewrite code unilaterally, the system surfaces the proposed refactoring for review. “The tool actually picks up those differences, and it will propose fixes,” Graykowski said. “It’s going to look at it and just say, &#8216;Okay, here’s the refactoring I’m proposing. Take a look at it. Do you approve?'&#8221;</p>
<p>That same approval model can support more autonomous regression repair, as long as the changes remain isolated until an engineer accepts them. Graykowski said one customer wanted an agent to analyze failures, make candidate fixes, rerun the regression, and return with a sandboxed result: “I’ve created a snapshot of your code, I’ve gone off, and I’ve worked on it in this sandbox. Here are the changes I’ve made. Do you approve these changes now?”</p>
<p>Darbari sees three emerging ways AI can reduce cross-tool friction, ranging from near-term optimization to deeper infrastructure changes. But he draws a sharp distinction between automation that preserves context and automation that simply adds another agent to the relay.</p>
<ul>
<li><b>Cross-boundary optimization loops.</b> This is the most mature AI use case in EDA — learning which settings, constraints, and tool sequences work together across comparable designs. The value is not that AI writes better code, but that it can reduce the reconciliation tax by learning and reusing combinations that improve productivity, compute efficiency, and PPA from RTL to GDSII.</li>
<li><b>Agentic pipelines and copilot layers.</b> Tools such as Synopsys.ai Copilot, Cadence ChipStack and AuraStack, and Siemens Fuse point toward a workflow layer that can connect architecture, RTL, verification, and physical design. But that layer needs safeguards. LLMs do not inherently understand native EDA data, design intent, production-security requirements, or the limits of their own outputs.</li>
<li><b>AI as an interoperability layer.</b> If the second layer orchestrates tools, the third gives agents a shared representation of what those tools produce. Vendor-neutral efforts such as Si2’s Schema Ontology and Accellera’s CDC/RDC Integration Standard point to abstractions that let agents reason across tools without rebuilding context at every step. Without that common substrate, AI may accelerate tool use but still lose meaning at the boundaries.</li>
</ul>
<p>For formal verification, AI is most valuable when handoff loss is high. “LLMs can extract properties, suggest assertions, propose abstractions, and triage proofs. However, AI outputs must be independently verified, as generated assertions are hypotheses, not proof. Only a completed proof against a correct property counts as evidence. A prompt is not proof,” Darbari said.</p>
<p>Cadence’s Graykowski noted that kind of checked assistance could also lower the barrier to formal verification for teams without deep formal expertise. If engineers can define intent or provide a specification, an agent can help generate candidate properties and check code before it reaches simulation or a formal engine such as Jasper. The point is not to replace formal expertise, but to move more designs toward machine-checkable evidence earlier in the flow.</p>
<p>Further, Darbari observed that single-tool AI features are becoming table stakes. “The next competitive frontier is between tools — agentic orchestration, standardized data models, and the ability to move constraints, waivers, and evidence across tool boundaries without loss. The <a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2607.17528v3">FluxBench evaluation</a> of AI agents attempting end-to-end RTL-to-GDSII is a sobering reminder that the seams are still hard. The problem is not the AI. It is the lack of a shared semantic substrate for the AI to reason over.”</p>
<p>The need for a shared semantic substrate is where orchestration becomes more than automation. The agent has to understand not only which tool to call next, but what each result means in the larger system context.</p>
<p>AI can provide an intelligent orchestration layer across EDA tools. “Rather than requiring an engineer to manually inspect every result and determine the next action, an AI agent can correlate information from multiple tools, understand the wider system context, and recommend or execute the appropriate next step,” Arteris’ Nightingale said. “For example, it could identify a system-level performance issue, relate that issue to an architectural or configuration decision, make a controlled change, and rerun the relevant analysis to determine whether the result has improved.”</p>
<p>A fundamental shift in AI&#8217;s evolution involves moving from operating inside individual tools to operating between tools. Standardized interfaces can make EDA capabilities accessible to agents, but tool access alone is not enough.</p>
<p>“AI also needs domain-specific context, a consistent representation of design intent, controlled permissions, and measurable results against which its actions can be checked. In this model, AI provides reasoning and orchestration while established EDA engines continue to provide deterministic analysis and verification,” Nightingale explained.</p>
<p>Rahim expects compute to keep moving up the stack, first from tools to workflows, and eventually from workflows into chip-design-specific models. Today’s frontier models are not yet specialized, cost-effective, or physically aware enough to generate fully verified, PPA-optimized RTL, analog layouts, advanced packaging, or netlists on demand. But he believes that capability will improve as models absorb more workflow knowledge and domain context. “We are confident we can tackle the problem because our customers are pulling us. Semiconductors are becoming a commodity. The number of projects they have to do, the number of layouts, and the analog experts they have available no longer scale. Because of that, our customers need a solution in that space, and they are looking for a partner to work with. They are willing to share a lot of that layout knowledge for us to train on.”</p>
<p>Additionally, Vinci&#8217;s Radhakrishnan said that AI can remove repetitive work around physics analysis by preparing inputs, invoking the right tools, carrying results forward, and comparing alternatives within engineer-defined boundaries. But the agent is only as useful as the analysis beneath it. If simulation still requires hours of manual setup and days to run, an AI front end does not solve the bottleneck. Agentic workflows become useful when the underlying analysis is fast, automated, deterministic, and production-scale.</p>
<p>In Vinci’s case, the approach is to ingest native design files and pair pretrained physics models with GPU-native numerical physics kernels, producing solver-accurate results without human meshing or customer-specific training data. Radhakrishnan said the point is not probabilistic simulation-by-chatbot, but repeatable physics results that can be used while the design is still changing.</p>
<div>
<p>Many companies are now using agentic AI or other types of AI to enhance workflows or optimize tools in the EDA process, as well as for other reasons. Mo Faisal, founder and CEO of <b>Movellus</b>, sees this as an advantage for new companies. “They&#8217;re starting from scratch, and I’m a little jealous of companies born in the last month. They don&#8217;t have the baggage, at least in Silicon Valley. The most common use I&#8217;ve seen is automatic customer ticket triage, customer success, and customer support. You put in the documentation and all of your context. When a customer ticket comes in, it is automatically processed, though there&#8217;s still a human in the loop. That workflow is probably the earliest in terms of benefiting from agentic AI first.&#8221;</p>
</div>
<div>
<p>From a product development point of view, agentic AI is being used to create product definition specs and do quick prototyping. “Product management is blurring with engineering,&#8221; Faisal observed. &#8220;Design is product management and engineering, so the workflow changes are happening there for the open-minded teams,” Faisal noted. “In other areas like legal and accounting, etc., that&#8217;s low-hanging fruit, but bringing agentic AI into complex engineering workflow- that&#8217;s the really interesting part here. It&#8217;s definitely happening. People have libraries of skill files now, so with whatever they&#8217;re doing for their workflow, they have a bunch of skill files that are skilled in a certain step; then models are called in as they&#8217;re processing that. Yet, while this is true in Silicon Valley, if you go somewhere else, it’s not happening yet.&#8221;</p>
</div>
<p><b>Raising the abstraction</b><br />
As the industry gains experience with AI, EDA workflows are likely to become increasingly intent-driven. “Rather than directly operating every tool and manually translating information between different environments, engineers will increasingly be able to specify objectives such as performance targets, connectivity requirements, security policies, or implementation constraints,” Nightingale said. “AI agents can then help determine which analyses and tools are required to meet those objectives and coordinate the necessary iterations across the design flow.”</p>
<p>This will make verification even more important. As agents are trusted to make larger changes and run longer workflows, every action will need an observable, verifiable outcome. “The most effective future EDA environments are therefore likely to combine AI-driven exploration and orchestration with deterministic engineering tools that continuously provide ground truth. The objective is not autonomous chip design for its own sake, but to reduce repetitive tool interactions and manual translation so engineers can spend more time making architectural and system-level decisions,” he said.</p>
<p>Radhakrishnan said the first challenge is to remove discrete bottlenecks, such as model preparation, analysis setup, and result comparison. Over time, those steps can become part of connected design loops in which an agent proposes a change, initiates the right physics analysis, checks the result against requirements, and either explores another option or sends the design to an engineer for review.</p>
<p>That would enable engineering teams to consider many more ideas. In fact, engineers who now test a handful of options may be able to examine hundreds or thousands, turning design exploration from a scheduled event into an iterative, more creative part of daily engineering work. But Radhakrishnan noted that the boundary between automation and human judgment will still matter. Early exploration may tolerate more autonomy, but validation and signoff require traceability, reproducibility, and deterministic results.</p>
<p>The longer-term opportunity is a design environment where AI agents coordinate specialized tools while deterministic physics keeps pace with the ideas engineers generate. In that model, physical behavior is evaluated throughout the flow, not only at scheduled checkpoints.</p>
<p>Axiomise’s Darbari pointed to visible shifts, each of which he expects to accelerate over the next two to three years. “The first shift is from tool-level AI to flow-level evidence. The first generation of AI in EDA sold productivity. The second will be judged on evidence. A signoff report that says, &#8216;The AI copilot converged the design in 40% less time,’ is interesting to a project manager. A signoff report that says ‘these properties are proven, these are bounded, these are AI-suggested and not yet checked, here is the reproducibility record,’ is what a safety, security, or automotive customer will accept. The current infatuation with autonomy will give way to an insistence on auditability. The second shift is occurring from simulation confidence to proof-backed signoff. The shift I care about most is from ‘we ran a lot of simulation, and everything looked green’ to ‘we can point at machine-checkable evidence for the properties that matter, and AI helped us get there faster.’ AI-assisted property extraction, agentic coverage closure, and LLM-driven abstraction discovery are real accelerators, but their output has to land on a formal engine that produces deterministic proof, or the confidence is theater. Apple&#8217;s Hilbert system, which wraps informal LLM reasoning around Lean 4, is the clearest public example of the architecture that will win. AI for exploration. Formal for correctness closure.”</p>
<p>Another wrinkle is that AI silicon splits into two verification and signoff regimes. “Training hardware lives or dies on distributed progress, collective operations, numerically valid reductions, and silent-data-corruption resilience across large clusters,” Darbari added. “Inference hardware, especially decode-heavy serving, lives on KV-cache ownership, scheduling, isolation, fairness, and tail latency. The cross-tool optimizations that matter for a training accelerator don&#8217;t matter for an inference tile. The AI-in-EDA story will fragment along the same lines. AI will not remove the need for handoffs. A boundary will always exist between architectural intent and implementation, between design and verification, and between pre-silicon proof and post-silicon behavior. AI can compress the reconciliation tax at each boundary and give engineers more time for the questions only humans can answer. Use AI for speed. Use formal for truth. Treat the boundaries between tools as places to accumulate evidence, not places to lose it.”</p>
<p>That shift from tool-level automation to flow-level evidence also changes what EDA companies and engineering teams have to organize around.</p>
<p><b>Organizational changes required</b><br />
Tool vendors face the same organizational challenge as their customers. Agents built inside individual product groups can recreate the silos they are supposed to remove. Synopsys’ Andersen said the shift has to be guided from the top, not left entirely to bottom-up experimentation. “Every product team tends to say, ‘I’m going to build an agent in my domain, but we have to look at the whole flow.”</p>
<p>That matters because agentic EDA will fail if it simply adds another layer of locally optimized automation. To reduce handoff loss, organizations need shared ownership of the end-to-end flow, common data and permission models, and metrics that measure whether agents improve engineering outcomes rather than merely execute more steps.</p>
<p>Rahim expects workflows to advance over the next six months, especially in root-cause analysis, verification, timing closure, physical design, analog, and advanced packaging. But he cautioned that complex, fully optimized designs remain beyond current frontier models. The likely path, he said, is gradual, with specialized workflows becoming more capable, workflow knowledge moving into model layers, and chip-design models becoming more physically aware through collaboration with customers and foundries.</p>
<p>Graykowski succinctly framed where AI belongs in this flow: “We’re leveraging these tools as assistants, not replacements. You have to guide it. They’re the junior engineer. You’re the senior engineer.”</p>
<p>That may be the most practical way to think about AI’s role in EDA. It will not eliminate the boundaries between specification, implementation, verification, signoff, packaging, and post-silicon learning. Nor will it make probabilistic answers acceptable where deterministic proof is required. Its value will come from what happens at those boundaries: whether agents can carry intent, assumptions, constraints, results, and proof across the flow without losing meaning. If they can, evidence-driven automation becomes more than a productivity story. It becomes the foundation for EDA workflows that execute faster, are easier to audit, and are safer to trust.</p>

		<title>AI-Driven Device Modeling For Next Generation Quantum Applications</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/ai-driven-device-modeling-for-next-generation-quantum-applications/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/ai-driven-device-modeling-for-next-generation-quantum-applications/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Fahad Usmani]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 24 Sep 2026 07:02:21 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - SLD]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[First By Design]]></category>
